Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images View image in fullscreen President Donald Trump greets supporters after speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Trump tariffs Trump is determined to pursue his trade war – and he may be difficult to stop Eduardo Porter The president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerous Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT Share Donald Trump may have found the killer weapon to punish countries at will: by imposing tariffs on their exports to the United States. The president has been looking for a new tool since February, when the supreme court struck down tariffs he slapped on virtually all of America’s trading partners based on the International Economic Emergency Powers Act, or IEEPA, on the spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies. It’s become a parlor game among policy wonks to predict what new legal justification he would deploy to replace them. Well, it’s probably not what you think. The round-robin tariffs imposed on everybody last Friday, under the argument that America’s trading partners unfairly undercut US companies by importing things made with forced labor, has drawn a lot of attention. The blatantly specious accusation, sitting uneasily alongside America’s own state-sanctioned abuse of forced labor , underscored how low Trump will stoop to get his way on trade. But those tariffs, imposed under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, do not provide the carte blanche Trump wants. Tariffs under this section are meant to retaliate against specific “acts, policies and practices” that are “unreasonable” and “burden or restrict” US companies. A blanket charge that every foreign country is enabling forced labor and thus hurting American business is unlikely to fly in court . The whole strategy can be challenged as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” or as “unsupported by substantial evidence”. The truly menacing precedent comes from Trump’s decision, made the Monday before the worldwide forced labor tariffs came into play, to foist a 50% tariff on imports from Canada. The White House’s pretext is Canadian discrimination against American dairy, booze and cars, which, paradoxically, came about as retaliation against Trump’s original barrage of tariffs last year. Sly observers, however, have pointed to Trump’s threat to punish Canada for the forest-fire smoke that wafted into the US. Maybe the new duties are meant to soften Canada as talks get under way to renew the USMCA North American trade pact, or to convince Canadians to become America’s 51st state. Or just because “tariff” is a pretty word . The authority Trump invoked to attack Canada is ominous: section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which is the law that choked global trade in the 1930s and helped sink the world into the Great Depression. Section 338 is particularly dangerous because it offers cover for the president to slap trade levies on whatever country he wants under some fairly hazy arguments. Specifically, it grants the president authority to retaliate against countries that do anything to put the United States “at a disadvantage compared with the commerce of any foreign country”. As soon as the president decides this is going on, he is authorized to “declare such new or additional rate or rates of duty as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage”. Until Trump, section 338 was never invoked to impose tariffs. It was mostly used as leverage, to guarantee that other countries treated American products the same as imports from anywhere else. If some country offered preferential access to a neighbor or ally, the US could demand the same terms, or else. This principle is now called “most favored nation treatment,” which is central to multinational trade rules enforced by the World Trade Organization. Trump doesn’t care about such niceties, though. He has a more destructive agenda in mind. And the statute appears to give him semantic wiggle room. He is determined to pursue his trade war. With such a sprawling mandate, he may be difficult to stop. America’s trading partners were elated in February when a 6-3 majority on the court, including two justices appointed by Trump, ruled against his use of the 1977 IEEPA to impose tariffs at will. It was close, though. The court has shown an almost unbelievable deference to the president. It didn’t object to Trump’s spurious invocation of national emergencies – a “public health crisis” due to illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico and China; trade deficits that “led to the hollowing out” of American manufacturing; something something because Brazil jailed its ex-president Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup. The justices merely objected to his use of the statute to impose taxes, which are the preserve of Congress. The executive has gotten away with similarly spurious arguments before. In 1975 President Richard Nixon was allowed to invoke the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 to slap tariffs on a zipper company from Japan, a country with which the US was not at war. Trump’s lawyers, in fact, argued before the supreme court that this precedent supported the president’s emergency powers to raise tariffs on anybody under IEEPA. Though Trump lost, his menace to the world remains. Since February his minions have trawled through legal statutes across American history to restore roadblocks to trade. Balance of payments crises don’t exist any more. Still, fresh from his supreme court loss, Trump imposed a 10% tariff on everybody by invoking section 122 of the 1974 act, which allows for tariffs to prevent such imbalances. The use of the law is so ridiculous that Trump’s own lawyers, in the IEEPA case, argued before the supreme court justices that section 122 could not be used as a substitute. In 1974, when the dollar’s exchange rate was fixed, a balance of payments crisis could happen when inflows of money from abroad couldn’t cover the trade deficit, forcing the government to sell foreign assets to plug the gap and preserve the exchange rate. These days the dollar floats. If too little money is coming in, it falls, making it cheaper and thus more attractive for foreigners to buy dollar assets, bringing things back into balance. Fortunately, the balance of payments tariffs had a statutory limit of 150 days. But Trump has tried other stuff too. Section 301 has been used many times before, including by Trump against China in his first term to penalize it for its industrial subsidies, which give its producers an unfair leg up. Trump has also relied on section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act to put levies on steel, aluminum, lumber, semiconductors and autos on specific grounds about protecting national security. None of these authorities, however, grant him the unrestrained blanket power that could be his under section 338. Let’s see what he does with it. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/202.text: Crime & Law Confusion and delays at district court as criminal legal aid dispute drags on Judge in midlands court adjourns dozens of cases and encourages some defendants to secure representation At Mullingar District Court, Judge Patricia Cronin adjourned the cases, noting the effect of the withdrawal of services. Photograph: Alan Betson/The Irish Times Stephen Farrell Sat Sept 12 2026 - 16:12 • 3 MIN READ Dozens of criminal legal aid cases were adjourned at a midlands district court on Thursday due to the withdrawal of services by criminal solicitors involved in the legal aid payment dispute . At Mullingar District Court , Judge Patricia Cronin adjourned the cases, noting the effect of the withdrawal. The dispute between criminal solicitors and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan over the rate of pay for free legal aid work has been continuing since O’Callaghan implemented the new system of a flat €520 fee per case. Under the previous system, solicitors received €240 for a first appearance and €60 thereafter, with some complex cases requiring a large number of hearings. The sense of confusion created by the dispute was evident at Mullingar, with a number of defendants, including non-nationals, appearing with no representation and apparently not knowing what free legal aid meant. READ MORE Ireland v Israel build-up live: Fixture to be fulfilled due to ‘significant majority’ in player vote Buckingham Village was supposed to reinvigorate Dublin’s inner city. By 2022, it was its worst slum Paddy McKillen jnr built a hospitality empire – now the man with €270 in the bank owes €27.7m Is Ireland ready for a monster El Nino? Expect ugly potatoes, transport chaos and widespread disruption One case involved a young Polish man who appeared before Cronin on “serious matters”, according to the judge. When asked by Cronin if he had a solicitor, he replied: “No, I’m alone.” When she further asked if he would like to apply for free legal aid, he replied, “what is that?” with the judge going on to explain the scheme to him. The young man, who earns €550 a week and who gives half of this to his mother, with whom he lives along with his brothers, was granted a certificate for free legal aid by Cronin. She told him that due to the dispute she was putting his case back and encouraged him in the meantime to seek legal advice as the alleged offences he faces may have “consequences” for him going forward. [ Taoiseach dismisses call for mediator in criminal legal aid dispute Opens in new window ] On Thursday the judge reminded those present on a number of occasions that it was the practice of the court to grant legal aid to suitable applicants without assigning a solicitor until one was in a position to come on record. When assessing eligibility for legal aid, Cronin asked applicants if they were working or in receipt of social welfare and how much their income was. Some of the free legal aid cases involved the appearance of defendants who were on bail, with the judge remanding them in custody on continuing bail to appear again in court, sometimes on a date as far away as December. In one case neither the defendant nor his solicitor were present in court; Cronin adjourned the case, with the State to notify the solicitor or the defendant of the next court date. One defendant who wished to have his case dealt with on the day did not apply for legal aid and entered a guilty plea to having €50 worth of cannabis for his own personal use. Cronin took into account his personal circumstances including that he has one dependent, that he pays €1,000 in rent and that his weekly income from his job is €750. She imposed a fine of €150 to be paid within three months. Whereas initially the solicitors’ strike was widespread, this resolve appears in some areas to be coming under strain. It has been reported that solicitors in counties Clare and Laois have formally concluded their strike, with criminal legal aid certificates being granted to solicitors in counties including Louth, Waterford, Limerick, Carlow, Tipperary and Kilkenny, but with the overall certificate numbers well below usual levels. People appearing before the courts over alleged criminal offences have a constitutional right to legal advice, including the right to a solicitor, even when they do not have the means to pay. https://www.dw.com/en/gerhard-schröder-v.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NvB4 Schröder's various board positions in Russia, not least at state energy giants, have caused considerable controversy in recent years, particularly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine Image: RBC/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement Gerhard Schröder visited one of the Moscow branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain on Wednesday, a few days after being named a member of its supervisory board. Russian TV footage showed employees at the branch greeting the former German chancellor and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, with sustained applause. Schröder has current or recent links to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin , issues that have become increasingly contentious in Germany in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 . Schröder was German chancellor when Vladimir Putin first became Russian president; the pair have remained close since he left office, despite all that followed Image: Alexei Druzhinin/dpa/picture alliance What is Hyperglobus' link to Germany? The new Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus was spun off from Germany's Globus Holding last year. Last week, Hyperglobus announced that Schröder had been appointed to the supervisory board. The supermarket confirmed that the former chancellor and Social Democrat had visited a branch on the western outskirts of Moscow on Wednesday. "I'm very pleased to be here, to see this wonderful hypermarket, to see the results of your work and to meet you, my wonderful colleagues," RBC television in Russia quoted Schröder as saying. Schröder and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, were greeted with sustained applause, Russian TV reported Image: RBC/Handout/REUTERS Schröder also reportedly called last week for the continuation of remaining trade ties between Russia and countries like Germany amid the sanctions imposed since the start of the war in Ukraine. "It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward," newspaper RBK reported him as saying last Friday. What's the deal with Schröder, Putin, Russia and Ukraine? Schröder's close ties to Putin came under scrutiny even while he was still in office, notably in 2004 when Schröder responded to a question from a reporter by saying that, yes, he believed Putin was a "flawless democrat" or lupenreiner Demokrat . Even 22 years ago, this assertion strained credulity in many eyes — not least among opposition groups or in war-torn Chechnya. On leaving politics, Schröder kept close ties to the Kremlin and took up a series of senior roles, perhaps most famously on the board of the Rosneft energy giant and before that on the board of the Nord Stream gas pipeline project that was majority owned by Gazprom. Putin has often said Schröder could negotiate a peace deal with Ukraine. Schröder, in turn, has declared himself willing. Image: Vladimir Rodionov/Ria Novosti/Kremlin Pool/dpa/picture alliance In 2014, not long after the annexation of Crimea and as a Russian-backed civil war brewed in Ukraine, Schröder was Nord Stream's guest of honor in St. Petersburg, where he celebrated his 70th birthday in lavish style. Four years later, after an election many in the West decried as bordering on a sham, Schröder took a prominent place at the 2018 swearing-in ceremony for Putin's fourth presidential term at the Kremlin (pictured above). Now-deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny once said Schröder was Putin's "errand boy." In 2024, Schröder was stripped of a state-funded office and staff — typically provided to former chancellors — on the basis that he was no longer fulfilling any obligations tied to his previous role in government. His party, the center-left Social Democrats, tried on several occasions to eject him as a member. Each attempt failed to clear the high legal bars required, and he remains a member, having joined in 1963. Putin has often suggested him as a possible peace mediator between Russia, Ukraine and Europe — with Schröder also expressing a willingness to take on the role — even though the reality is he would likely be entirely unacceptable as a mediator to all parties other than Russia, and particularly to Ukraine. By Tom O'Connor Deputy Editor, National Security and Foreign Policy 0 Share Newsweek is a Trust Project member See more of our trusted coverage when you search. Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search. Growing tensions surrounding the Russia-Ukraine war risk bringing the conflict within NATO’s borders, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has warned. “We do not disregard the risk of the Russia-Ukraine war spreading to a wider region,” Erdogan told Newsweek in an exclusive interview. “Allegations of sabotage and hybrid activities in Europe are also adding to the fragility of the current security environment.” His comments came as fellow NATO leaders and top officials intensified warnings of a suspected effort by Russia to test the alliance’s resolve in continuing support for Ukraine. Read More on News ... Erdogan urged caution, however, asserting that it was Ankara’s role to seek de-escalation rather than pursue bellicose measures. “In this process, it is necessary to act with restraint, assess the allegations on the basis of solid evidence and avoid steps that could further escalate tensions,” Erdogan said. “Türkiye’s priority is to prevent the war from turning into a conflict that draws in other countries.” Newsweek Members can read the exclusive interview in full . Russia-NATO 'Hybrid War' Fears Rise Instances of the war’s spillover into NATO territory have been reported since early in the conflict that erupted with Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, largely in the form of missiles and drones falling into neighboring countries. But reports of incidents have spiked over the past year, particularly since nearly two dozen drones said to be of Russian origin penetrated Polish airspace in September 2025. Since then, dozens of drone sightings have been reported across European nations, often with authorities pointing to suspected involvement of Russia, which has consistently denied responsibility. In one of the most high-profile incidents, Germany held Russia directly responsible after an explosive drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August. In the weeks since, Romania, Moldova and Lithuania have reported new drone sightings on their respective territories, with NATO jets downing a drone believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Russian ally Belarus in mid-September. Related Story The New ‘Muslim NATO’ Faces First Major Test Another drone spotting in Germany on September 23 led to the closure of Berlin’s airspace for around 45 minutes. As European officials increasingly sound alarms of a potential “hybrid warfare” campaign being waged by the Kremlin, other murky episodes have also raised suspicions. They include twin attacks on electrical substations in Germany and an apparent act of sabotage against a railway in the Netherlands, though no link to Russia has been established in these cases and German investigators have identified a climate activist as the main suspect in the substation attacks. Still, European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas warned that “Europe faces a fast proliferation of sabotage attacks and airspace violations,” through which “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. “As Russia is willing to take greater risks, Europe must impose greater costs,” Kallas said. ... Meanwhile, Russian officials have accused European countries of pursuing their own hybrid campaign against Moscow, including through growing military aid to Ukraine, sanctions against Russian trade and other measures. Speaking in September, Russian Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Dmitry Polyansky asserted that Moscow had repeatedly confirmed that it “has no plans to attack the EU or NATO,” despite an ongoing European military build-up and other measures “that risk escalating the hybrid war against Russia into a conventional war.” Why Turkey's Position Matters With NATO leaders calling for harsher action against Russia, Erdogan has emerged as a leading proponent of mediation. And Ankara’s record shows a clear ability to bring the warring sides to the table. Just five weeks into Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Turkey launched the Istanbul peace talks and, despite the absence of a war-ending deal, went on to oversee elusive agreements between Moscow and Kyiv, such as the July 2022 Black Sea deal to safeguard crucial grain exports from Ukraine and several prisoner swaps. ... “Türkiye’s position on the Russia-Ukraine war has remained unchanged for over four years,” Erdogan said. “The Istanbul talks, the Black Sea Grain Initiative and prisoner exchanges are tangible outcomes of our ability to engage with both sides. Türkiye is a strong NATO Ally. “At the same time, we are able to maintain direct contact with both President Putin and the Ukrainian leadership. I see no contradiction in this,” Erdogan said. “To mediate, you need to be able to talk to both sides of a conflict.” Erdogan’s channel to Putin had previously been activated to conduct talks on other conflicts, including those in Syria, Libya and the Caucasus. The war in Ukraine marked a particular test, however, as Turkish-made drones provided Kyiv’s forces with an early edge against Moscow’s invasion. Still, the two men remain in contact, having most recently met in September at the Kyrgyzstan-hosted summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a Eurasian organization into which Turkey entered as a dialogue partner in 2013 and remains engaged. During the meeting, Erdogan said he “made it clear that Türkiye stands ready to do its part to help achieve peace.” And despite early success in Black Sea arrangements, Erdogan said that the security of this maritime theater remains an issue to which Turkish officials “attach particular importance” as Ankara seeks a new, more comprehensive framework to pacify these shared waters. ... Erdogan said his government was prepared to move forward with a new dialogue between Russia and Ukraine—provided that the two countries’ leaders signaled willingness to resume talks to put an end to Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II. Erdogan’s offer comes amid renewed diplomatic efforts by U.S. President Donald Trump to end the war. “As the war continues, its humanitarian, economic and political costs continue to grow,” Erdogan said. “Once the necessary political will is demonstrated, Türkiye stands ready to contribute to bringing the parties back to the negotiating table and paving the way for peace.” Neither East nor West Erdogan’s quest to position Turkey as a pillar of diplomatic influence goes beyond easing Russia-NATO tensions. Erdogan noted Turkey’s efforts to advance ties not only with the SCO, but also other multilateral blocs such as the Organization of Turkic States, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, the G-20 and the D-8 Organization for Economic Cooperation. Ankara is also pressing forward with a number of regional development projects that would increase connectivity with China and the Persian Gulf. Erdogan said that “Türkiye’s unique position between East and West naturally calls for a multidimensional and multifaceted foreign policy.” ... This outlook becomes all the more important given that Turkey is beset not only with a war raging in Ukraine across from its Black Sea shores, but across its land border with Iran, against which the U.S. and Israel launched a war in February. Turkey is far from immune from the profound disruptions in regional security and global energy trade that have ensued, adding impetus to de-escalate on this front as well. “The world is going through profound shifts,” Erdogan said. “The Russia-Ukraine war continues to our north. Conflicts to our south and east directly affect our region’s security, economy and stability. At times like these, it is the collective responsibility of the international community to expand the space for diplomacy rather than narrow it.” And that’s where he said Turkey fits in as a nation capable of resisting pressure to maintain rigid alignments while simultaneously exploring new forms of cooperation in line with what Erdogan views to be a rapidly evolving international order. “We pursue our national interests, regional stability and global peace in tandem,” Erdogan said. “While preserving our long-standing alliances, we forge new partnerships and, when necessary, bring different centers of power together around the same table.” Related Story Erdogan’s New World Order: Turkey Won’t Choose East or West View 0 Comments Request Reprint & Licensing Submit Correction View Editorial & AI Guidelines

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6e3.text: Image source, Getty Images By Aleks Phillips Published 4 hours ago A man suspected of a deadly gun attack near Paris has left custody and been placed under psychiatric observation, French anti-terrorism officials have said. One person was killed and five others injured on Friday when an attacker opened fire from his car - first in Trappes, and then in nearby La VerriÃ¨re - appearing to target people of migrant origin. The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said. President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack", adding that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion. It marked a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation", the French president said. Figure caption, Watch: Emergency services at the scene of the shooting on Friday PNAT said the move to place the suspect under psychiatric evaluation followed guidance from a psychiatric expert. The evaluation will determine whether the suspect should remain in police custody and is "likely to last 48 hours", PNAT added. PNAT said the suspect was also found to have cannabis and cocaine in his bloodstream. French newspaper Le Monde , external and news agency AFP report that a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf were found at the suspect's home, citing a source close to the investigation. The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare". He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately. Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday. The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up. "His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts." Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition. The mayor of La VerriÃ¨re, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better". Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said. The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged". He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.
